content.p: On 30 November 2022, a FedEx contract driver delivered a box of Barbie dolls to a house in Paradise, Texas. The dolls were a Christmas present for a seven-year-old girl named Athena Strand. Within the hour, according to the sheriff, the driver had taken her from the family's land and killed her. Her body was found two days later.

The driver, Tanner Lynn Horner, pleaded guilty to capital murder and aggravated kidnapping on 7 April 2026, on the day his trial was due to begin. A Tarrant County jury then spent about a month hearing evidence on punishment, and on 5 May 2026 it sentenced him to death. His appeals are only starting.

Athena was taken from her father's rural property in Paradise, in Wise County, near Fort Worth. Her mother, Maitlyn Gandy, of Oklahoma, had sent the Christmas present, a box of "You Can Be Anything" Barbies. Athena's stepmother, Ashley Strand, told the jury that Athena loved the country property, where she got to "run wild and free".

Horner was a contract driver for FedEx Ground, employed through a subcontractor, Big Topspin, Inc., according to the lawsuit later filed by Athena's family. Wise County Sheriff Lane Akin said he did not know the family or the child. On 30 November 2022 he arrived at the Strand home with the package.

Shortly before Athena's stepmother realised the girl was missing, the sheriff said, Horner had dropped off the parcel. Authorities looked at who had delivered to the address around the time she vanished. According to the arrest warrants, Horner's own employer, a FedEx subcontractor, tracked him down, and surveillance video from his truck showed the child inside, talking to him.

Gandy has said she begged for an AMBER Alert from the moment she reached her daughter's father's property, but told legislators in April 2023 that it was not sent until about 24 hours later. Several Texas school districts wore pink in the following days, pink being Athena's favourite colour, according to CNN and CBS News Texas.

Horner was questioned and led investigators to the child's body, then surrendered without incident, according to a warrant quoted by CNN. Authorities said she was found about 9 miles from her home, southeast of Boyd. CBS News Texas reported that Horner first gave detectives two false locations. Digital evidence and interviews led investigators to believe she died within an hour of being taken, Akin said. He was held on a $1.5 million bond on capital murder and aggravated kidnapping charges.

Horner's account to the police, as described in the warrants, was that he had backed his truck into Athena by accident, that she was not seriously hurt, and that he panicked. He said he put her in the vehicle and killed her because she was going to tell her father she had been hit by the truck. Prosecutors would later call that story a lie.

Later in December 2022, charging documents made public by CNN showed three unrelated sexual assault charges against Horner out of Tarrant County, dating to 2013. The documents did not identify the alleged victims, who were minors. NBC 5 reported in February 2023 that he was being held on four such charges. They were separate from the Strand case.
content.h2: Charges, a death notice and a move to Fort Worth
content.p: A Wise County grand jury indicted Horner on 16 February 2023 for aggravated kidnapping and capital murder of a person under 10, CBS News Texas reported. District Attorney James Stainton filed notice the next day that he would seek the death penalty. Gandy's lawyers told her a capital case usually takes 18 months to two years to come to trial.

It took far longer. In November 2025, on the third anniversary, CBS News Texas reported that no trial was expected before spring 2026 because of venue changes and other delays. Horner had pleaded not guilty in 2023. His lawyers argued he could not get a fair trial in Wise County, and the case moved to Fort Worth. Jury selection was scheduled to begin on 1 April 2026, with the trial set for 7 April.

On 7 April 2026 Horner pleaded guilty to capital murder, and to aggravated kidnapping. A guilty plea to capital murder leaves a Texas jury a narrow choice, which was between death and life in prison without parole. The trial went straight to the punishment phase.

In his opening statement Stainton rejected the version that Horner had given investigators. "The only truthful thing that Tanner Horner told law enforcement was that he killed her," he said. "It is lie upon lie upon lie upon lie." He told jurors that Athena had not been injured when Horner put her in the truck, and that Horner's DNA was found under her fingernails. Defence lawyer Steven Goble conceded that the evidence against his client was "overwhelming" and "terrible". He asked jurors to consider that Horner's mother drank during her pregnancy, that he has autism and had suffered from "various mental illnesses", and that he had been exposed to "a massive amount of lead".

The sentencing phase ran for weeks; ABC7 and FOX 9 put it at about a month. Witnesses included Athena's stepmother, her father and her mother. Jacob Strand told jurors that after his daughter's death he turned to alcohol, his marriage fell apart, and "I lost 50 pounds".

Christy Jack, a Texas lawyer who has handled death penalty cases, told CBS News Texas that the most impactful evidence was the audio tape, which was recorded in the truck. Prosecutors showed video of Horner covering and uncovering a dash camera with what appeared to be a sticky note, which they said he also did on the day Athena was taken. Cameras inside the cab showed him preparing the back of the truck, and later picking Athena up and putting her inside. Stainton told jurors that Horner told her not to scream or he would hurt her. After he covered the second camera, the audio kept running for more than an hour. On the recording, according to the AP, Athena asked why he was doing this and asked for her mother. The judge cleared cameras from the courtroom when the audio was played. Her parents were not present.

A medical examiner, Dr Jessica Dwyer of the Southwestern Institute of Forensic Sciences, testified that Athena died from blunt force injuries with smothering and strangulation. She told the jury that the examination found no evidence of sexual trauma but that some sexual contact remained possible. Prosecutors presented evidence that Horner sexually assaulted Athena before strangling her, and in closing, Stainton called that the act of a "true predator". Horner's earlier version, in which he killed her after she saw him using cocaine, was also among the accounts prosecutors dismissed as fabrication, CBS News Texas reported.
content.h2: The defence and the stories Horner told
content.p: Horner's account changed over time. Texas Rangers investigator Job Espinoza testified that in interviews Horner referred to an alter ego he called "Zero" and said he had made it up. Espinoza described engaging with "Zero" as an interview technique to get information and find Athena. In a jail letter shown to jurors, written during a suicide attempt in May 2023, Horner apologised to Athena's family and blamed his autism and trouble at work and at home. In a second letter, for detectives only, he claimed that a stranger with a rifle had forced him to take the child. Prosecutors told the jury that Horner continued to lie into January 2026.

The defence called expert witnesses on his mental health and medical history. Horner's mother and grandmother described his childhood. Lead lawyer Susan Anderson reminded jurors of his diagnoses of fetal alcohol spectrum disorder, ADHD and autism, and asked them for mercy. "Tanner's problems began before he was even born," she said. Stainton told the jury that experts who had never expected Horner to hurt a child "were wrong, absolutely wrong".

Before closing arguments on 5 May, the defence asked the judge to take the death penalty off the table because of the international attention the trial had received, and said that the defence team, witnesses and Horner had received death threats. The judge denied the motion.

The jury was asked two questions. The first was whether Horner would be a continuing threat to society. Its answer was yes. The second was whether any mitigating circumstances justified life without parole rather than death. Its answer was no. Under Texas law the answers made a death sentence mandatory, Judge Gallagher said as he read the order.

Sources differ on how long the jurors took. KSL said over two hours, FOX 9 about two and a half hours, and CBS News Texas and others less than three. During deliberations the jury asked to see the videos, a letter from an inmate and the rape kit, and the judge allowed those three requests, FOX 9 reported. Horner, who was 34, stood and showed no visible reaction. He was to remain in the Tarrant County Jail until moved to the Texas Department of Corrections in Huntsville. NBC News said the judge sentenced him to be executed before sunrise on a date to be set.

After the sentence was read, Athena's uncle, Elijah Strand, addressed Horner. "You did not just take a life; you destroyed a family," he said. "I want you to know," he said, "that you are nothing. You are a footnote in Athena's story. Her name will forever be remembered, her name will forever be celebrated, and everyone will forget you." Stainton, whom FOX 9 described as handling his first death penalty case, said both he and the family felt the verdict was justice.

Texas death sentences are appealed automatically to the Court of Criminal Appeals, and the judge said a lawyer would be appointed for that appeal. CBS News Texas reported a notice of appeal filed on 6 May, which it took to be the automatic one, and another that it dated 11 May. Neither came with further documents. The process can also include a state habeas review, in which claims based on facts outside the trial record, such as ineffective counsel, can be raised, and later federal review. Jack, speaking to CBS News Texas, estimated that it would be at least twice as long as the three and a half years since the killing before any execution. No execution date has been set.

In December 2022, Athena's father, Jacob Strand, sued Horner, FedEx and Big Topspin. The suit sought more than $1 million and accused the companies of gross negligence and of negligent hiring, including failing to investigate Horner's criminal history and mental health. FedEx said it was aware of the complaint and that its thoughts were with the family. Gandy filed her own wrongful death suit in February 2023.

Gandy also pushed for House Bill 3556, known as Athena's Alert, a localised alert that would go to people within about 100 miles of where a missing child was last seen. She told her story to Texas legislators in April 2023, while stressing that it would not replace the AMBER Alert. By November 2025, CBS News Texas reported that the alerts had taken effect and were helping police get out information about missing children more quickly. Mattel also gave Cook Children's Medical Center in Fort Worth a donation of 2,000 Barbies in her honour, NBC 5 reported.
